GATE-STYLE MCQ • Binary Search Tree  |  07/15
What is the worst-case time complexity of searching in an ordinary, unbalanced BST containing n keys?
A.  O(1)
B.  O(log n)
C.  O(n)
D.  O(n log n)

ANSWER & JUSTIFICATION • Binary Search Tree  |  07/15
Correct Answer: C. O(n)
JUSTIFICATION
If keys are inserted in sorted order, the BST can become skewed with height n − 1. A search may then inspect every node.
GATE TIP: BST operations are O(height), not always O(log n).

GATE-STYLE MCQ • Binary Search Tree  |  08/15
In a BST, the keys in the left subtree of a node x are:
A.  Greater than x only
B.  Less than x only
C.  Less than or equal to x in every implementation
D.  Unrelated to x

ANSWER & JUSTIFICATION • Binary Search Tree  |  08/15
Correct Answer: B. Less than x only
JUSTIFICATION
Under the standard distinct-key BST convention, every key in x’s left subtree is less than x, and every key in its right subtree is greater than x. Duplicate-key policies vary by implementation.
GATE TIP: The BST ordering constraint applies to the entire subtrees.

GATE-STYLE MCQ • Binary Search Tree  |  09/15
A BST has root 25, left child 15, right child 40, and node 15 has children 10 and 20. What is the inorder sequence of these five nodes?
A.  25, 15, 10, 20, 40
B.  10, 15, 20, 25, 40
C.  10, 20, 15, 40, 25
D.  40, 25, 20, 15, 10

ANSWER & JUSTIFICATION • Binary Search Tree  |  09/15
Correct Answer: B. 10, 15, 20, 25, 40
JUSTIFICATION

text:
Inorder is left subtree, root, right subtree. The left subtree yields 10, 15, 20; then 25; then 40.
GATE TIP: Apply the traversal order recursively.

GATE-STYLE MCQ • Heap  |  10/15
A max-heap is represented in a zero-indexed array. For the node at index i, its left-child index is:
A.  2i
B.  2i + 1
C.  2i + 2
D.  ⌊i/2⌋

ANSWER & JUSTIFICATION • Heap  |  10/15
Correct Answer: B. 2i + 1
JUSTIFICATION
For a zero-indexed array representation, the left child of index i is at 2i + 1 and the right child is at 2i + 2, if those indices exist.
GATE TIP: Do not confuse zero-indexed and one-indexed formulas.

GATE-STYLE MCQ • Heap  |  11/15
Which statement is true for every max-heap?
A.  The array is sorted in descending order
B.  Every parent is greater than or equal to its children
C.  The left child is always greater than the right child
D.  The root is the minimum key

ANSWER & JUSTIFICATION • Heap  |  11/15
Correct Answer: B. Every parent is greater than or equal to its children
JUSTIFICATION
A max-heap enforces a local parent-child ordering. It does not require siblings or the full array to be sorted; the root stores a maximum element.
GATE TIP: Heap order is not the same as sorted order.

GATE-STYLE MCQ • Heap  |  12/15
What is the time complexity of inserting one key into a binary max-heap with n existing elements?
A.  O(1) worst case
B.  O(log n) worst case
C.  O(n) worst case
D.  O(n log n) worst case

ANSWER & JUSTIFICATION • Heap  |  12/15

source: GATE_Binary_Trees_BST_Heap_15_MCQ (1).pptx
text:
Correct Answer: B. O(log n) worst case
JUSTIFICATION
The new key is appended at the next available leaf and may sift up along the heap height. A binary heap has height O(log n).
GATE TIP: Insertion performs at most one upward path.

GATE-STYLE MCQ • Heap  |  13/15
What is the worst-case time complexity of building a binary heap from n arbitrary elements using bottom-up heapify?
A.  O(log n)
B.  O(n)
C.  O(n log n)
D.  O(n²)

ANSWER & JUSTIFICATION • Heap  |  13/15
Correct Answer: B. O(n)
JUSTIFICATION
Bottom-up heap construction heapifies internal nodes from the last parent toward the root. Most nodes are near the leaves and require little work; the total is O(n), not O(n log n).
GATE TIP: Bottom-up build-heap is linear time.

GATE-STYLE MCQ • Heap  |  14/15
A max-heap array is [90, 70, 80, 20, 50, 60]. After deleting the maximum and restoring the heap, what is the resulting array?
A.  [80, 70, 60, 20, 50]
B.  [80, 70, 60, 20, 50, 90]
C.  [70, 60, 80, 20, 50]
D.  [80, 50, 70, 20, 60]

ANSWER & JUSTIFICATION • Heap  |  14/15
Correct Answer: A. [80, 70, 60, 20, 50]
JUSTIFICATION
Remove root 90, move the last element 60 to the root, then sift down. Since 60 is less than its larger child 80, swap; now 60 is greater than its children 20 and 50. The heap becomes [80, 70, 60, 20, 50].
GATE TIP: Delete-max replaces the root with the final array element, then sifts down.

GATE-STYLE MCQ • Heap  |  15/15

Which data structure is most suitable for repeatedly retrieving the largest element while allowing efficient insertion?
A.  Unsorted linked list
B.  Binary max-heap
C.  Stack
D.  Binary search tree with no balancing guarantee

ANSWER & JUSTIFICATION • Heap  |  15/15
Correct Answer: B. Binary max-heap
JUSTIFICATION
A max-heap provides O(1) access to the maximum at the root, and O(log n) insertion and delete-max. An unbalanced BST can degrade to linear time.
GATE TIP: Priority queues are commonly implemented using binary heaps.

Queue (Linear Queue)
Example:
         Queue:  AAA, BBB, CCC, DDD, EEE


Using an array as a queue.


How to Handle Queues?
One possibility is an array. The advantages to arrays are that they're easy to use and that adding an item to the end of an array's filled portion is easy. 
The problem comes with removing an item from the front of the queue. 
Array Implementation of Linear Queue

source: grk_final queue.pptx
text:
Memory wastage : The space of the array, which is used to store queue elements, can never be reused to store the elements of that queue because the elements can only be inserted at front end and the value of front might be so high so that, all the space before that, can never be filled.

Deciding the array size: On of the most common problem with array implementation is the size of the array which requires to be declared in advance. Due to the fact that, the queue can be extended at runtime depending upon the problem, the extension in the array size is a time taking process and almost impossible to be performed at runtime since a lot of reallocations take place. 

Removing an item from the front of the queue
Removing an item from the front of the queue consists of 
copying the value of the first element of the array (simple) and then 
moving each item left in the array one element toward the front. 
Although this is easy to program, it wastes a lot of computer time

Vacated elements become dead space
Second way: In array implementation, leave the remaining elements where they are and change which element you call the front.  
The sequence of Addqueue and DeleteQueue operations, drifts towards the end of the array solution: Circular queue. wrapping around from the end of the array to the beginning.






Circular Queue is used to avoid having this end as barrier. 
Implemented using Modulo arithmetic Operation
		Front := Front + 1 mod Qsize
		Rear   := Rear  + 1 mod Qsize

Theorem
Let T be a nonempty, full binary tree Then:
If T has I internal nodes, the number of leaves is L = I + 1.
If T has I internal nodes, the total number of nodes is N = 2I + 1.
If T has a total of N nodes, the number of internal nodes is I = (N – 1)/2.
If T has a total of N nodes, the number of leaves is L = (N + 1)/2.
 If T has L leaves, the total number of nodes is N = 2L – 1.
If T has L leaves, the number of internal nodes is I = L – 1.
If T has I internal nodes, the number of leaves is L = I + 1.   	
If T has I internal nodes, the total number of nodes is N = 2I + 1.        
If T has a total of N nodes, the number of internal nodes is I = (N – 1)/2.
If T has a total of N nodes, the number of leaves is L = (N + 1)/2.
 If T has L leaves, the total number of nodes is N = 2L – 1.
If T has L leaves, the number of internal nodes is I = L – 1.

A prefix expression is an algebraic expression in which each binary operator precedes its two operands:
				+ a b             (a+b)
				+ a * b c       (a+(b*c))
				* + a b c       ((a+b)*c)

text:
We can use the procedure 'Heapify' in a bottom-up fashion to convert an array A[1 . . n] into a heap. Since the elements in the subarray A[n/2 +1 . . n] are all leaves, the procedure BUILD_HEAP goes through the remaining nodes of the tree and runs 'Heapify' on each one. The bottom-up order of processing node guarantees that the subtree rooted at children are heap before 'Heapify' is run at their parent.

	 Buildheap(A)
	{         heapsize[A] 🡨length[A]         for i 🡨|length[A]/2  //down to 1            do Heapify(A, i)  } 

‹#›
HEAP SORT ALGORITHM
The heap sort algorithm starts by using procedure BUILD-HEAP to build a heap on the input array A[1 . . n]. Since the maximum element of the array stored at the root A[1], it can be put into its correct final position by exchanging it with A[n] (the last element in A). If we now discard node n from the heap than the remaining elements can be made into heap. Note that the new element at the root may violate the heap property. All that is needed to restore the heap property.

	Heapsort(A)
	{         Buildheap(A)         for i 🡨 length[A] //down to 2             do swap A[1] 🡨🡪 A[i]             heapsize[A] 🡨 heapsize[A] - 1             Heapify(A, 1) } 

‹#›
HEAPIFY
HEAPIFY — Local correction (bottom-up repair) 
Purpose:Heapify(A, i) ensures that the subtree rooted at index i satisfies the heap property (for a max-heap → parent ≥ children), assuming the left and right subtrees are already heaps.
It’s a local repair operation.

BUILD-HEAP — GLOBAL CONSTRUCTION
Purpose: Build-Heap(A) converts an unordered array into a valid max-heap (or min-heap).
It repeatedly calls Heapify from the last internal node up to the root
How it works: Starts from the last internal node (n/2) Moves upward toward the root Each call to Heapify fixes a subtree

HEAP SORT — Extraction + reheapification
Purpose: To sort an array in ascending order using a max-heap. It repeatedly removes the largest element (root of heap) and places it at the end of the array

*
‹#›
HeapSort(A)
   └── Build-Heap(A)
          └── Heapify(A, i)
TIME ANALYSIS
Build Heap Algorithm will run in O(n) time
There are n-1 calls to Heapify each call requires O(log n) time
Heap sort program combine Build Heap program and Heapify, therefore it has the running time of O(n log n) time
Total time complexity: O(n log n)


‹#›
POSSIBLE APPLICATION
When we want to know the task that carry the highest priority given a large number of things to do

Interval scheduling, when we have a lists of certain task with start and finish times and we want to do as many tasks as possible

Sorting a list of elements that needs and efficient sorting algorithm

CONCLUSION
The primary advantage of the heap sort is its efficiency.

A matrix is just a table with rows and columns. If most values are zero, we call it a sparse matrix. Why do we use it?

A matrix is a two-dimensional data object made of m rows and n columns, therefore having total m x n values. If most of the elements of the matrix have 0 value, then it is called a sparse matrix.

Why to use Sparse Matrix instead of simple matrix ?
Storage: There are lesser non-zero elements than zeros and thus lesser memory can be used to store only those elements. Saves memory: Instead of storing so many 0’s, we only save useful (non-zero) numbers
Computing time: Computing time can be saved by logically designing a data structure traversing only non-zero elements. Faster calculations: The computer skips over 0’s and only looks at important numbers.

A sparse matrix contains many zero values and only a few non-zero values. Therefore, instead of storing the entire matrix, we store only the non-zero elements. For every non-zero element, we normally store three details:  its row number,  its column number, and  its value.
10 non-zero elements. Therefore, the normal list representation requires 30 entries: 10 row numbers, 10 column numbers, and 10 values. However, the elements are stored row by row. So, instead of repeating the row number for every element, we store only the starting position of each row. 

Row 1 starts at position 1   Row 2 starts at position 3 , Row 3 starts at position 7,   Row 4 starts at position 8,  Row 5 has no non-zero element, so it is marked as 0, Row 6 starts at position 9.
Thus, the row list needs only 6 entries instead of 10 entries. The column and value lists still contain 10 entries each. Therefore, the total storage is:
6 row entries + 10 column entries + 10 value entries = 26 entries.
If each entry occupies 2 bytes, the memory required is:   26 × 2 = 52 bytes.
Originally, 30 entries were required. Now only 26 entries are required. Therefore, we save 4 entries by using sequential representation. The main idea is simple: because the elements are stored row by row, we need to store only where each row begins.”

 CSR (Compressed Sparse Row) - Yale Format
The CSR (Compressed Sparse Row) or the Yale Format is similar to the Array Representation of Sparse Matrix. 
We represent a matrix M (m * n), by three 1-D arrays or vectors called as A, IA, JA. 
Let NNZ denote the number of non-zero elements in M 
0-based indexing is used. 
A for storing actual values.
IA for telling us where each row starts.
JA for column positions.This is a very compact and fast way to store huge matrices in computers

CSR format uses three arrays:
A → stores actual non-zero values.
JA → stores column indices of those values.
IA → tells us where each row starts in A (like an index guide).
Row 0 → all zeros (no non-zero values).
Row 1 → has 5, 8 (2 non-zeros).
Row 2 → has 3 (1 non-zero).
Row 3 → has 6 (1 non-zero).
So total NNZ (non-zero count) = 4.
JA Vector (Column Indices)
JA = [0, 1, 2, 1]
5 is in column 0 → JA has 0
8 is in column 1 → JA has 1
3 is in column 2 → JA has 2
6 is in column 1 → JA has 1
IA Vector (Row Start Indexes)
IA has m+1 elements (here rows = 4, so IA size = 5).
It is defined like this:
IA[0] = 0
IA[i] = IA[i-1] + (non-zero count in row (i-1))
Step by step:
IA[0] = 0
IA[1] = IA[0] + non-zeros in row 0 = 0 + 0 = 0
IA[2] = IA[1] + non-zeros in row 1 = 0 + 2 = 2
IA[3] = IA[2] + non-zeros in row 2 = 2 + 1 = 3
IA[4] = IA[3] + non-zeros in row 3 = 3 + 1 = 4
So IA = [0, 0, 2, 3, 4]
Why do we need IA?
It tells us where each row’s data begins in the A and JA vectors.
Row 0 → IA[0] = 0, IA[1] = 0 → no entries.
Row 1 → IA[1] = 0, IA[2] = 2 → entries from index 0 to 1 in A & JA.
Row 2 → IA[2] = 2, IA[3] = 3 → entry at index 2.
Row 3 → IA[3] = 3, IA[4] = 4 → entry at index 3.
So IA is like a row pointer table.
JA says: which column each non-zero belongs to.
IA says: where each row’s data starts and ends in JA.

Python Solution

def validate(pushed, popped):
    stack, j = [], 0
    for x in pushed:
        stack.append(x)
        while stack and stack[-1] == popped[j]:
            stack.pop()
            j += 1
    return not stack
The while loop handles several pops in a row
